title: When instructions become an algorithm
goal: State a contract, trace the steps and distinguish a correct answer from a program that merely stops.

prerequisites.text: You can identify a problem's inputs and outputs.
Division with remainder helps but C++ syntax is not a prerequisite.

sections.title: Turn an informal task into precise steps
paragraphs: The label “125 seconds” does not tell you how to format the display. Agree on two fields: full minutes on the left and 0–59 leftover seconds on the right. Both fields matter.
The instruction “convert seconds to minutes” leaves a question: what should happen to the remainder? For 125 seconds we want two integers: 2 whole minutes and 5 seconds.

Start with 0 minutes and a remainder of 125. While the remainder is at least 60, subtract 60 from it and add one minute. Print the resulting minutes and remainder. Both the step and the stopping rule are now precise.
Predict the result for 59 and 60 seconds before writing code. There are no subtractions for 59 and exactly one for 60. This checks that the condition includes equality.

sections.title: Definiteness and discreteness
paragraphs: Discreteness means reasoning about a computation as a sequence of individual steps. Definiteness means the executor can identify the intended operation at each step.

First read the number of seconds. If extraction fails, there is no value to calculate with: print invalid and stop. Then check the sign. Only after these two steps divide by 60: / gives whole minutes and % gives the remaining seconds.

Try oops in place of the number of seconds. Extraction fails before the sign check. This is a different reason for rejection from reading -1 successfully and then rejecting its value. Both branches must stop before division.
trace: Extraction succeeded and the value is non-negative.
steps: Dividing 125 by 60 gives 2 and leaves a remainder of 5. The output 2 5 follows the agreed order.
One minute and 65 seconds also total 125 seconds. That pair fails the remainder rule.
125 seconds equals two minutes and five seconds.
The remainder is less than 60 for a nonnegative input.
Never apply remainder reasoning to division by zero.
The program halts after reporting the pair.

sections.title: Termination, the input domain and generality
paragraphs: A terminating algorithm must finish for every input in its stated domain. A condition such as n >= 0 matters: a loop designed for positive counts may misbehave outside that domain.
Generality means solving a class of related instances, not a single hard-coded example. A sound addition algorithm should work for multiple valid pairs.
Try 0, 59 and 60 seconds. The results 0 0, 0 59 and 1 0 follow the same rule. At 60 the number of whole minutes changes; a negative value is rejected before calculation.

sections.title: Correctness requires more than stopping
paragraphs: Imagine the program stops at one minute and a remainder of 65. The total is still 125, but 65 seconds contains another whole minute. Halting alone tells you nothing about whether the answer is correct.

Trace the pairs (minutes, remainder): (0, 125) → (1, 65) → (2, 5). Each added minute compensates for the 60 seconds subtracted. The equality 60 × minutes + remainder = original seconds holds at the start and after each step. A property preserved this way is called an invariant.

We subtract 60 only from a remainder of at least 60, so the remainder stays nonnegative. When the condition becomes false, 0 ≤ remainder < 60. Together with the invariant, this gives the required postcondition. Would the equality alone be enough?

sections.title: Identify an exit condition before coding the loop
paragraphs: A nonnegative quantity that strictly decreases often explains termination. But you must check that each transition actually reduces the quantity under the preconditions.
Changing a loop requires revisiting its invariant and exit condition. Forgetting to update a counter can turn a correct finite loop into an infinite one.

Return to the remaining seconds. Every step decreases the remainder by exactly 60 and keeps it nonnegative. There cannot be infinitely many such subtractions. If you remove the subtraction, the test “remainder ≥ 60” stays true for 125.

sections.title: Contract and postcondition
paragraphs: A timer shows 125 seconds. A report needs whole minutes and the seconds left over. Which two numbers will the reader see?
Write both numbers before running the program. Then check whether they reconstruct the original time.

reveal.title: Compare your prediction and trace the steps
paragraphs: For 125 seconds, the result is 2 minutes and 5 seconds: 125 = 60·2 + 5. Zero produces 0 and 0. The general postcondition is seconds = 60·minutes + remainder with 0 ≤ remainder < 60. Integer / gives the quotient and % the remainder. Once nonnegative input has been checked, these operations match ordinary division.

Division and remainder produce the same result as repeated subtraction. Check reconstruction and the remainder bound. The pair 1 65 reconstructs 125, but violates the bound and is therefore incorrect.
steps: 125 seconds equals two minutes and five seconds.
The remainder is less than 60 for a nonnegative input.
Never apply remainder reasoning to division by zero.
The program halts after reporting the pair.

sections.title: Input policy and execution limits
paragraphs: Integer inputs must fit the Code Studio int type. Failed extraction (text instead of a number or end of input) produces invalid; no further calculation is performed.

Supply the stated number of whitespace-separated integer tokens. Extra tokens are outside this small input contract. Keep a record of source, exact stdin, predicted output and observed output. These examples introduce the logic; the following modules develop C++ types, streams and functions in depth.

sections.title: Try a separate task
paragraphs: Pack a nonnegative number of parts into boxes of 12. Print the full boxes and leftover parts separated by a space. Print invalid for a negative, missing or unreadable count.
Predict the first case and one boundary case. Practice has a separate starter. After running it, explain which check or operation produced each result.

selfcheck.prompt: Supply 61 seconds. What will the displayed program print?
feedback: 61 cannot be the remainder because it still contains a whole minute.
That would be the result for 60 seconds. One second remains.

selfcheck.prompt: What property makes each step unambiguous?
selfcheck.feedback: The executor can determine the next operation without guessing.

selfcheck.prompt: How does correctness differ from termination?
options: An algorithm may halt and return a wrong result
selfcheck.feedback: Finishing and producing the required result are separate obligations.

options: A number that must always be positive
selfcheck.feedback: An invariant supports reasoning about intermediate states.

selfcheck.prompt: Why is checking only 12 × boxes + leftover = 29 insufficient? Give an incorrect pair that still totals 29.
selfcheck.feedback: One box and 17 loose parts total 29, but 17 parts can fill another box. Explain both the total and the 0–11 remainder rule. This explanation is not graded automatically.

practice.title: Full boxes and leftover parts
practice.task: Pack a nonnegative number of parts into boxes of 12. Print the full boxes and leftover parts separated by a space. Print invalid for a negative, missing or unreadable count.
criteria: Check extraction and nonnegativity before calculating.
Check 12 × boxes + leftover = the original count and 0 ≤ leftover < 12.
Explain the result of one new valid case before running it, then compare with the observation. Matching output alone does not assess understanding.
practice.hint: Name both parts of the result and check them separately for input 11.

exercises.task: After solving the task, test 23 and 24 parts separately. Predict both lines before running.
exercises.criteria: 23 → 1 11; 24 → 2 0. One more part fills the second box and resets the remainder to zero.

exercises.task: Predict both output fields for 0, 59, 60 and 125 seconds. Then check that a negative value and unreadable input are rejected before calculation.
exercises.criteria: For valid values: 0 0; 0 59; 1 0; 2 5. Explain 60 × minutes + remainder = seconds and 0 ≤ remainder < 60. Rejected input produces invalid.

exercises.task: Write four boundary tests for age validation.
exercises.criteria: Include both endpoints and two invalid inputs.

exercises.task: Justify the result of converting seconds into minutes and a remainder.
exercises.criteria: For accepted input, seconds = 60*minutes + remainder and 0 <= remainder < 60.

passport.knowledge:
Definiteness — The intended action of each step is unambiguous.
Invariant — A property that remains true across specified state transitions.
Postcondition — A property that must hold when the algorithm finishes.
passport.change: Pack a nonnegative number of parts into boxes of 12. Print the full boxes and leftover parts separated by a space. Print invalid for a negative, missing or unreadable count.
passport.result: Source, exact input and actual stdout. If output files are specified, check their contents separately.
passport.checks:
Check extraction and nonnegativity before calculating.
Check 12 × boxes + leftover = the original count and 0 ≤ leftover < 12.
passport.errors: Name both parts of the result and check them separately for input 11.
passport.recovery: Keep the failing version separately. Compare the first differing step with the walkthrough; fix one cause and repeat an ordinary and a boundary case. Opening the reference does not replace your code.
